questions.question: Q1. In the simulation you ran an SfM reconstruction with 8 input images arranged in a full 360-degree ring around the object (45° apart) and achieved a sparse point count of 2400 with reprojection error 0.6px. You then ran the same object with the same 8 images but clustered within a narrow 60-degree arc. Reprojection error stayed similar (0.65px) but the reconstructed point positions showed significantly higher position uncertainty, especially in depth. Explain this discrepancy.

answers.a: The clustered configuration should have performed identically since both used exactly 8 images with similar reprojection error
answers.b: Reprojection error measures how well the 2D image observations match the projected 3D points, but does not directly measure 3D triangulation precision. In the clustered 60° configuration, all viewing rays converge at very similar shallow angles, creating poor triangulation geometry — small pixel-level matching errors translate into large 3D position uncertainty because the rays are nearly parallel rather than well-separated, exactly analogous to narrow stereo baseline effects in Experiment 1
answers.c: The full ring configuration failed while the clustered configuration succeeded, contradicting standard SfM practice
answers.d: Clustering images always improves accuracy since the images are more similar to each other and easier to match

explanations.a: Not quite. While both configurations achieved similar low reprojection error (meaning the 2D observations fit the model reasonably well in image space), this metric alone does not capture 3D triangulation quality — the actual observed result shows a clear difference in 3D position uncertainty between the two configurations despite similar reprojection error.
explanations.b: Correct! Reprojection error is a 2D image-space metric — it measures how closely the projected 3D points match their observed 2D image positions. It can remain low even when the underlying 3D triangulation is poorly constrained, because a poorly-triangulated point can still project close to its correct 2D position in each image while having substantial uncertainty along the depth direction. In the clustered 60° arrangement, all camera viewing rays toward a given 3D point are nearly parallel (narrow triangulation angle), meaning the geometric intersection used to determine depth is poorly constrained — a small angular or pixel-matching error causes the computed intersection point to shift substantially along the ray direction. This is the direct multi-view generalisation of the stereo baseline effect from Experiment 1, where a narrow baseline (small triangulation angle) produces large depth uncertainty for the same disparity measurement error. The full 360° ring configuration provides wide, diverse triangulation angles at every point, producing well-constrained (low uncertainty) 3D positions even with the same reprojection error level.
explanations.c: Not quite. Neither configuration failed in the sense of not producing a reconstruction — both produced point clouds with similar reprojection error. The distinction is specifically about the precision/uncertainty of the resulting 3D positions (particularly in depth), not about whether reconstruction succeeded or failed outright.
explanations.d: Not quite. This is the opposite of the correct relationship. While clustered, similar images might indeed be easier to match feature correspondences between (due to similar appearance), this ease of matching does not translate to better 3D accuracy — in fact, as demonstrated, the resulting triangulation geometry is weaker, producing higher 3D position uncertainty despite potentially easier matching.

questions.question: Q2. You configured the simulation with 12 images at 75% consecutive overlap, achieving 94% surface coverage in the final dense reconstruction. You then reduced overlap to 35% while keeping the same 12 images spread around the same object. Coverage dropped to 58%, with several visible gaps in the reconstructed surface. Explain the mechanism causing this coverage reduction, referencing the minimum multi-view visibility requirement.

answers.a: Lower overlap always causes the entire reconstruction to fail completely rather than producing partial coverage with gaps
answers.b: At 35% overlap, many surface regions are captured by only one image (or briefly transition through zero overlapping images) as the camera moves between viewpoints, meaning those regions never achieve the minimum two-image visibility required for triangulation — these under-covered regions appear as gaps in the final reconstruction, while the well-overlapped regions between viewpoint transitions still reconstruct successfully
answers.c: The 35% overlap result is identical to the 75% result, and the coverage difference must be attributed to a separate unrelated cause
answers.d: Overlap percentage only affects processing speed, never actual coverage completeness

explanations.a: Not quite. As directly observed in the scenario, reduced overlap produced partial coverage with specific visible gaps (58% coverage, not 0%), rather than complete reconstruction failure. Regions that do maintain adequate overlap still reconstruct successfully; only the specific under-covered regions fail to reconstruct.
explanations.b: Correct! As camera viewpoints move around the object with only 35% overlap between consecutive images, there are larger angular gaps between successive camera positions. Surface regions near the edges of each image's field of view — particularly those visible in only the current image but not yet visible in the next image due to insufficient overlap — fail to achieve the minimum two-image visibility requirement described in the theory (Section 5) needed for triangulation. As the theory explicitly states, every 3D point must be visible in at least two images to be triangulated at all. With only 35% overlap, more of the object's surface falls into this single-image-only category at various points during the camera's path around the object, directly producing the observed gaps. The 75% overlap configuration, by ensuring most surface points remain visible across several consecutive viewpoints, avoids this problem and achieves much higher coverage.
explanations.c: Not quite. The scenario explicitly describes different coverage outcomes (94% vs 58%) between the two overlap configurations — these are clearly different, not identical, results, and the theory provides a direct, well-established mechanism (the two-image minimum visibility requirement) explaining exactly this kind of difference.
explanations.d: Not quite. This directly contradicts the observed and theoretically explained result. Overlap percentage has a direct and substantial effect on reconstruction coverage completeness, as explicitly demonstrated by the significant coverage drop, and processing speed considerations are a separate concern from geometric coverage completeness.

questions.question: Q3. In the simulation you deliberately introduced 15% false feature matches (incorrect correspondences) into an otherwise clean 10-image dataset. Without RANSAC-based outlier rejection enabled, the bundle adjustment produced a visibly distorted, warped reconstruction with reprojection error 4.2px. With RANSAC enabled (correctly configured), reprojection error dropped to 0.4px and the reconstruction appeared geometrically correct. Explain the mechanism by which RANSAC achieves this improvement.

answers.a: RANSAC works by averaging all feature matches together, including the false ones, to produce a smoothed compromise result
answers.b: RANSAC repeatedly samples small random subsets of candidate matches, fits a geometric model (such as the fundamental matrix) to each subset, and identifies which candidate matches are consistent (inliers) versus inconsistent (outliers) with the best-fitting model across many trials — the false matches, being geometrically inconsistent with the true camera geometry, are identified as outliers and excluded before bundle adjustment runs, preventing them from corrupting the joint optimisation
answers.c: RANSAC physically retakes the photographs with a different camera to avoid the false matches
answers.d: RANSAC has no actual effect on reconstruction quality and the improvement must be attributed to a different, unrelated cause

explanations.a: Not quite. Averaging false matches together with correct matches would not remove their corrupting influence — it would simply blend the error into the result rather than eliminating it. RANSAC's actual mechanism is specifically designed to identify and exclude outliers, not to average them into a smoothed compromise.
explanations.b: Correct! RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus, referenced in the theory Section 7) works by repeatedly selecting small random subsets of the candidate feature matches, fitting a geometric model (such as the fundamental matrix relating an image pair, per the epipolar geometry from Section 3) to each subset, and then checking how many of the OTHER candidate matches are consistent with that fitted model within some tolerance. The subset (and corresponding model) that achieves the highest number of consistent matches across many random trials is selected as the best geometric model, and all matches inconsistent with this winning model are classified as outliers and discarded. Since the deliberately introduced false matches do not correspond to any genuine, geometrically consistent camera relationship, they are very unlikely to be consistent with the correct fundamental matrix and are therefore correctly identified and excluded as outliers before the cleaned set of matches proceeds to bundle adjustment, preventing the false matches from corrupting the joint optimisation and explaining the dramatic reprojection error improvement observed.
explanations.c: Not quite. RANSAC is a purely computational, statistical algorithm operating on already-captured image data and candidate matches — it involves no physical action, camera operation, or new photography. It is applied entirely during the data processing stage after all images have already been captured.
explanations.d: Not quite. This directly contradicts the dramatic, clearly measured improvement described in the scenario (reprojection error dropping from 4.2px to 0.4px), which is a substantial and mechanistically well-explained consequence of RANSAC's outlier rejection process.

questions.question: Q4. You ran the simulation twice on the same object: Run A captured 15 images with good overlap but all from camera heights within a narrow 10-degree elevation range (essentially all photos taken from roughly the same height, circling only horizontally). Run B captured 15 images spanning a full range of elevation angles from directly above to nearly level with the object, in addition to horizontal circling. Run B produced noticeably more complete reconstruction of the object's top surface. Explain this difference in terms of visibility and camera network geometry.

answers.a: Run A and Run B should produce identical results since both used exactly 15 images
answers.b: Run A's narrow elevation range means every camera views the object from roughly the same vertical angle, so the top surface of the object (visible primarily from higher elevation viewpoints) is poorly observed or entirely absent from all 15 images — these points cannot be triangulated regardless of how much horizontal overlap exists, since visibility (a point actually appearing in the image) is a prerequisite for correspondence matching and triangulation, which horizontal-only camera diversity cannot provide for a surface that specifically requires elevated viewing angles
answers.c: Run B performed worse because more diverse camera angles always make feature matching harder and less reliable
answers.d: Elevation angle has no effect on which parts of an object are visible in a photograph

explanations.a: Not quite. While both runs used the same total image count (15), the scenario explicitly describes different camera network geometries (narrow elevation range vs full elevation range) between the two runs, producing measurably different reconstruction completeness specifically for the object's top surface — image count alone does not determine outcome; the geometric distribution of viewpoints matters critically.
explanations.b: Correct! This extends the camera network geometry principle (Section 6) to the specific case of surface visibility rather than triangulation angle precision. If every camera in Run A is positioned at roughly the same elevation, none of them have a clear, direct view of the object's top surface — a surface oriented mostly horizontally is best observed from viewpoints positioned above or nearly above it, looking somewhat downward. Without any camera positioned at a sufficiently elevated angle, the top surface may simply never appear clearly in any of the 15 images, or appear only at such an oblique, grazing angle that feature detection and matching becomes unreliable there. Since visibility in at least two images is an absolute prerequisite for triangulation (as established in Q7 of the pretest and Section 5 of the theory), no amount of horizontal camera diversity or overlap can compensate for the complete absence of appropriately elevated viewpoints — the top surface points simply cannot be reconstructed if no camera ever clearly observes them. Run B's inclusion of elevated viewpoints directly addresses this by providing cameras that can actually see and photograph the top surface clearly.
explanations.c: Not quite. This is the opposite of the general principle established in Section 6 — camera viewpoint diversity, including elevation diversity, generally improves reconstruction quality and completeness (by providing better triangulation geometry and broader surface visibility), not the reverse. Run B's more diverse elevation range directly produced better, more complete results, not worse ones.
explanations.d: Not quite. This directly contradicts basic photographic and geometric principles — the angle from which a camera views a 3D object fundamentally determines which surfaces of that object are visible and clearly photographed. A camera positioned level with an object cannot see its top surface clearly, exactly as the observed simulation result demonstrates.

questions.question: Q5. In the simulation you performed a reconstruction and then attempted to measure a known physical distance on the reconstructed model (a ruler placed in the scene, actually 30cm long) which measured as 45.2 arbitrary reconstruction units in the raw SfM output. You then measured a second known object (a 15cm reference cube edge) which measured as 22.6 reconstruction units. Verify whether these two measurements are internally consistent with a single scale factor, and explain what this consistency (or inconsistency) reveals about the underlying SfM reconstruction.

answers.a: The two measurements cannot be compared in any meaningful way since SfM reconstructions have no internal consistency at all
answers.b: Scale factor from ruler: 30cm/45.2units ≈ 0.664 cm/unit. Scale factor from cube: 15cm/22.6units ≈ 0.664 cm/unit. These two independently-derived scale factors agree closely, confirming that the SfM reconstruction correctly preserved consistent RELATIVE proportions throughout the scene (as expected, since relative geometry is what SfM directly recovers), even though determining the ABSOLUTE scale required this external reference measurement — exactly illustrating the scale ambiguity concept from the theory
answers.c: The two measurements should never match since every measurement in an SfM reconstruction uses a completely independent, unrelated scale
answers.d: This test proves the SfM reconstruction failed since two different objects gave two different raw unit measurements

explanations.a: Not quite. This dismisses a genuinely meaningful and standard verification technique used in practice — comparing scale factors derived from multiple independent known references is exactly how practitioners validate that an SfM reconstruction's relative geometry is internally self-consistent before trusting derived measurements.
explanations.b: Correct! Computing the scale factor from each reference independently: ruler gives 30/45.2 ≈ 0.6637 cm per reconstruction unit; cube gives 15/22.6 ≈ 0.6637 cm per reconstruction unit. These two values agree closely (both approximately 0.664), which is exactly what should be expected if the SfM reconstruction correctly and consistently preserved the true relative proportions of the scene throughout the entire reconstructed volume — the ruler and cube, despite being different objects in different locations within the scene, both scale by the same consistent factor when converted from raw reconstruction units to real centimetres. This directly and concretely illustrates the theory's scale ambiguity concept: the SfM pipeline alone correctly determined relative geometry (hence the consistent scale factor across different objects) but had no way to independently determine that its internal reconstruction units corresponded to 0.664cm each — this had to be established using an external known-size reference, exactly as the theory describes as the standard method for resolving scale ambiguity.
explanations.c: Not quite. This directly contradicts the fundamental principle that SfM correctly recovers relative geometric proportions throughout a single consistent reconstruction — if every measurement used an unrelated scale, the reconstruction would be geometrically meaningless internally, which is not the case for a properly functioning SfM pipeline, as confirmed by the consistent scale factors calculated here.
explanations.d: Not quite. The two raw unit measurements (45.2 and 22.6) being numerically different is entirely expected and correct, since the ruler (30cm) and cube edge (15cm) are physically different lengths — what matters for validating reconstruction quality is whether the SAME scale conversion factor applies to both, which it does (both ≈0.664 cm/unit), confirming success rather than failure.

questions.question: Q6. You ran the simulation comparing bundle adjustment convergence with 5 images (180 total feature correspondences) versus 25 images (2400 total feature correspondences) of increasing scene complexity. The 5-image case converged to reprojection error 0.3px in 12 optimisation iterations. The 25-image case required 340 iterations to converge to a similar 0.35px reprojection error, and the per-iteration computation time was also substantially longer. Explain why bundle adjustment computational cost scales so dramatically with image count, connecting this to the theory's description of the optimisation problem.

answers.a: Bundle adjustment cost should not increase with image count at all, and this result indicates a computational inefficiency bug
answers.b: As described in the theory (Section 4), bundle adjustment jointly optimises the position of every 3D point AND the pose of every camera simultaneously — with 25 images there are far more camera poses to solve for (25×6 degrees of freedom vs 5×6) and typically far more triangulated 3D points from the additional correspondences, dramatically increasing both the number of unknown variables and the number of reprojection error terms in the objective function E=ΣᵢΣⱼ||xᵢⱼ−π(Cⱼ,Xᵢ)||², making the joint optimisation problem substantially larger and more computationally demanding, consistent with the theory's description of bundle adjustment as 'computationally the most expensive stage of the SfM pipeline'
answers.c: The increased iteration count proves that using more images always produces a worse quality result
answers.d: Bundle adjustment computational cost depends only on image resolution, not on the number of images used

explanations.a: Not quite. Increasing computational cost with image count is the expected, theoretically predicted behaviour of bundle adjustment, not evidence of a bug. The theory explicitly identifies bundle adjustment as 'computationally the most expensive stage of the SfM pipeline' precisely because of this scaling behaviour with problem size (number of cameras and points).
explanations.b: Correct! Bundle adjustment's objective function E=ΣᵢΣⱼ||xᵢⱼ−π(Cⱼ,Xᵢ)||² sums over every 3D point i and every camera j — meaning the total number of terms being minimised grows with both the number of points and the number of cameras. Going from 5 to 25 images means 5× as many camera pose unknowns (each contributing 6 degrees of freedom: 3 rotation + 3 translation, as stated in Section 4), and since more images typically also enable more feature correspondences to be found and triangulated (as reflected in the jump from 180 to 2400 correspondences), the number of 3D point unknowns also grows substantially. This dramatically increases the total dimensionality of the joint optimisation problem being solved, which directly explains both the much higher iteration count needed for convergence and the longer computation time per iteration (since each iteration must process many more variables and error terms), fully consistent with the theory's explicit characterisation of bundle adjustment as the pipeline's most computationally demanding stage.
explanations.c: Not quite. Both configurations converged to a similarly low, good-quality reprojection error (0.3px vs 0.35px) — the increased iteration count reflects increased computational problem size and complexity, not a decrease in final reconstruction quality. More images with proper bundle adjustment generally improve reconstruction completeness and robustness, even though they increase computational cost.
explanations.d: Not quite. While image resolution can also affect computational cost (more detected features, more precise pixel coordinates), the scenario explicitly demonstrates a dramatic cost increase driven by image COUNT (5 vs 25 images) with the associated increase in camera poses and 3D points to solve for — this is a distinct and significant factor from image resolution alone, as explicitly described in the theory's discussion of the joint optimisation problem's scale.

questions.question: Q7. You configured the simulation with a highly repetitive textured surface (a brick wall pattern) and observed that even with RANSAC enabled, feature matching produced a higher-than-normal false match rate (28%, compared to 5% for a non-repetitive control surface), though RANSAC still successfully cleaned most of these before bundle adjustment. Explain why repetitive textures specifically challenge the feature matching stage, and discuss a limitation of RANSAC's ability to fully compensate for this.

answers.a: Repetitive textures have no effect on feature matching difficulty since all image features are matched using identical criteria regardless of texture pattern
answers.b: Repetitive textures like a brick wall pattern contain many locally similar-looking regions (individual bricks with near-identical appearance), causing feature descriptors from Stage 1 to be genuinely ambiguous — a feature on one brick can look nearly identical to a feature on a different brick, causing legitimate feature-matching confusion rather than random noise. While RANSAC can identify and reject matches that are geometrically INCONSISTENT with the majority consensus model, it may struggle specifically when a substantial fraction of the false matches happen to be geometrically PLAUSIBLE (for example, matching brick #5 to brick #7 might still satisfy epipolar geometry reasonably well if the repeating pattern has a very regular spacing), since RANSAC's core mechanism relies on outliers being geometrically inconsistent, not on all false matches being detectable this way
answers.c: RANSAC always achieves 100% correction of false matches regardless of the underlying cause of those false matches
answers.d: Repetitive textures only affect the dense reconstruction stage (Stage 6) and have no impact on earlier pipeline stages

explanations.a: Not quite. This ignores a well-documented and genuine challenge in feature matching — feature descriptors are designed to capture the local visual appearance around a keypoint, and when multiple locations in a scene share very similar local appearance (as with repetitive textures), the descriptors for those locations become similarly ambiguous, genuinely increasing the difficulty and error rate of correctly identifying corresponding matches.
explanations.b: Correct! Feature descriptors computed in Stage 1 encode the local visual appearance around each detected keypoint. On a highly repetitive surface like a brick wall, many different physical locations (different individual bricks) have very similar local visual appearance, causing their computed feature descriptors to be nearly indistinguishable from each other. This creates genuine ambiguity during matching — the algorithm may confidently but incorrectly match a feature on one brick to a similar-looking feature on a completely different brick, rather than the true corresponding feature. This differs from random matching noise because these errors are systematic and appearance-driven. Critically, RANSAC's fundamental mechanism (Section 7) works by identifying matches that are geometrically inconsistent with the best-fitting model — but if the repetitive pattern has regular, predictable spacing, a mismatch between similar-looking but different bricks might still approximately satisfy reasonable epipolar geometry constraints (especially if the mismatch is to a nearby repeated pattern element with a plausible offset), making such false matches harder for RANSAC to distinguish from true matches purely on geometric consistency grounds. This represents a genuine, partially unresolved limitation of RANSAC's outlier rejection approach specifically for the class of errors caused by repetitive scene texture, distinct from purely random mismatches which RANSAC handles more reliably.
explanations.c: Not quite. This directly contradicts the scenario's explicit description of a challenging case — while RANSAC generally performs well and did clean 'most' matches in this scenario, the framing of the question specifically explores why complete, perfect correction cannot always be guaranteed, particularly for the specific case of geometrically-plausible false matches arising from repetitive texture patterns.
explanations.d: Not quite. Repetitive texture challenges arise specifically at the feature detection and matching stages (Stages 1 and 2), which occur early in the pipeline, well before the dense reconstruction stage (Stage 6). If feature matching produces errors due to repetitive texture, this affects camera pose estimation (Stage 3) and sparse reconstruction (Stage 4) directly, propagating forward to affect later stages including dense reconstruction, rather than being isolated only to the final dense stage.

questions.question: Q8. You designed a comprehensive test comparing an SfM-only reconstruction of a mechanical part against a combined SfM+structured-light (Experiment 6) approach, following the theory's closing point about combining photogrammetry with dedicated depth sensors. SfM alone achieved good overall shape (relative accuracy) but with absolute measurement error of ±3.2mm across the part due to scale ambiguity resolved only approximately via a rough ruler reference. The combined approach used structured light's directly-measured absolute depth to anchor the SfM reconstruction's scale precisely, achieving ±0.15mm absolute accuracy. Explain the complementary strengths being combined in this hybrid approach.

answers.a: Combining two techniques always simply doubles the error of using either technique alone, so the combined approach should have performed worse, not better
answers.b: SfM contributes broad, flexible multi-viewpoint coverage and can capture complex full-object geometry relatively easily using ordinary photographs, but suffers from scale ambiguity requiring an external reference (Section 8) which, if approximate (a rough ruler measurement), limits absolute accuracy. Structured light contributes precise, directly-measured absolute depth at each measurement (via the phase-to-height formula from Experiment 6, not requiring any external scale reference) but has a more limited field of view and requires more controlled capture conditions. Combining them lets structured light's direct absolute measurements anchor and calibrate the SfM reconstruction's scale with high precision, while SfM's broader multi-viewpoint flexibility fills in overall shape and coverage that would require many separate structured-light captures to achieve alone — each technology compensating for the other's specific limitation
answers.c: The combined approach only worked because structured light completely replaced SfM rather than actually being combined with it
answers.d: This comparison is meaningless since SfM and structured light measure completely unrelated physical properties with no possible relationship between their outputs

explanations.a: Not quite. This directly contradicts the described outcome, where the combined approach achieved dramatically BETTER absolute accuracy (±0.15mm) than SfM alone (±3.2mm) — this demonstrates a complementary strength combination, not an error-doubling effect. Well-designed multi-sensor fusion approaches specifically aim to have each technology compensate for the other's weaknesses, which is exactly what is illustrated here.
explanations.b: Correct! This exemplifies the theory's closing point (Section 9) about real-world 3D reconstruction projects combining photogrammetry with dedicated depth sensors, using each technology's strengths to compensate for the other's limitations. SfM's strength is its flexibility and ease of achieving broad multi-viewpoint coverage using just ordinary photographs, efficiently capturing complex overall geometry — but its fundamental weakness (Section 8) is scale ambiguity, since photographs alone provide no absolute measurement reference, and an approximate manual reference (a rough ruler) only provides similarly approximate absolute accuracy. Structured light's strength (Experiment 6) is that its phase-to-height formula h=(p×φ)/(2π×tan α) directly computes absolute physical height measurements using known system geometry (fringe period, baseline angle) without requiring any external scale reference at all — but structured light's weakness is its comparatively limited field of view per capture and its need for controlled lighting conditions, making full-object coverage more effortful than with flexible SfM photography. By combining them, the structured light measurements provide a precise absolute scale anchor for the SfM reconstruction (resolving SfM's scale ambiguity far more precisely than a rough ruler could), while SfM's broader, more flexible coverage efficiently captures the complete object shape that would otherwise require many separate structured-light setups to achieve alone.
explanations.c: Not quite. The scenario explicitly describes a combined approach where structured light's absolute measurements anchor/calibrate the SfM reconstruction's scale, implying both techniques contribute to the final result (SfM providing broad shape coverage, structured light providing scale precision) rather than one completely replacing the other.
explanations.d: Not quite. This is factually incorrect — both SfM and structured light ultimately produce 3D geometric measurements of the same physical object (in this case, a mechanical part), making a direct and meaningful comparison and combination of their outputs both possible and, as demonstrated, practically valuable for achieving results neither technique alone could match.

questions.question: Q9. You ran the simulation with a fixed 20-image dataset and progressively increased the number of images randomly excluded from the reconstruction (simulating capture failures), from 0 excluded up to 12 excluded (leaving only 8 usable images), tracking sparse point count at each level. Point count decreased smoothly from 0 to 8 excluded, then dropped sharply and reconstruction became patchy/disconnected between 8 and 12 excluded. Explain this nonlinear degradation pattern using the concept of a connectivity graph between overlapping images.

answers.a: Point count should decrease at a perfectly constant linear rate regardless of how many images are excluded, and any nonlinearity indicates a simulation error
answers.b: With a full 20-image set arranged with good overlap, the images form a well-connected graph where most images share overlap with several neighbours, providing redundant paths for triangulation, so removing a moderate number of images (up to a threshold) still leaves enough overlapping connections for most surface points to remain triangulable via alternative image pairs. Beyond a certain removal threshold, the remaining images' overlap connections become sparse enough that the connectivity graph starts to fragment into disconnected components — some surface regions lose ALL adequate image coverage simultaneously, causing the sharp, nonlinear point-count drop and patchy/disconnected reconstruction observed between 8 and 12 excluded images
answers.c: Excluding images from an SfM dataset has no effect on reconstruction quality as long as at least one image remains
answers.d: The nonlinear pattern only occurs due to a hardware limitation of the specific computer running the simulation

explanations.a: Not quite. There is no theoretical reason to expect perfectly linear degradation — the underlying structure being degraded (a network of overlapping image connections providing multiple redundant triangulation paths) is not a simple linear system, and threshold/critical-transition behaviour is a well-established and expected characteristic of network connectivity problems generally, not evidence of simulation malfunction.
explanations.b: Correct! A well-captured SfM dataset can be conceptually modelled as a graph where each image is a node, and an edge connects two images if they have sufficient overlap to share matched features and support triangulation for their commonly-visible surface regions. With the full 20-image dataset providing good overlap (per Section 5's guidelines), this graph is well-connected — most surface points have multiple redundant image-pair connections available for triangulation, meaning losing a few images still leaves alternative overlapping pairs that can still triangulate the same surface points. This explains the smooth, gradual point count decrease for moderate exclusion levels (0 to 8 excluded) — redundant connections absorb the loss without catastrophic failure. However, as more images are removed, the graph's connectivity becomes progressively sparser, and eventually a critical threshold is crossed where certain surface regions lose their last remaining adequate-overlap connections all at once — this is a classic network fragmentation phenomenon where a graph maintains reasonable connectivity as edges are gradually removed until a critical point where it suddenly fragments into disconnected pieces. This directly explains both the sharp point-count drop and the emergence of patchy, disconnected regions in the reconstruction observed between 8 and 12 excluded images in the scenario — corresponding surface areas that were only weakly connected (few redundant overlapping image pairs) to begin with are the first to lose all coverage as the graph fragments.
explanations.c: Not quite. This contradicts the result described in the scenario, where excluding images clearly and substantially affected reconstruction quality, particularly showing a sharp degradation once sufficient images were removed — the theory's discussion of the minimum two-image visibility requirement and overlap guidelines throughout make clear that image exclusion has real, significant consequences for reconstruction completeness.
explanations.d: Not quite. The nonlinear, threshold-like degradation pattern described is a general, mathematically-grounded property of network/graph connectivity under progressive edge or node removal, applicable to any implementation of this scenario regardless of the specific hardware running the computation — it reflects genuine underlying structure in the overlap-connectivity relationships between images, not a computer-specific artefact.

questions.question: Q10. Reflecting across the entire 10-experiment lab, explain how SfM (Experiment 10) serves as a capstone that demonstrates the value of understanding fundamental principles (triangulation, calibration, correspondence, filtering) independent of any specific sensing technology, rather than learning each experiment as an isolated technique.

answers.a: Each experiment in this lab teaches completely separate, unrelated skills with no meaningful connections between them, and SfM is simply one more isolated technique unrelated to the rest
answers.b: SfM demonstrates that the core mathematical and geometric principles taught throughout this lab — triangulation from multiple viewpoints (Experiment 1), reprojection error minimisation and calibration (Experiment 2), point cloud generation and structure (Experiment 3), correspondence-based alignment (Experiment 4), and outlier-robust estimation (Experiment 8) — are not tied to any single sensing technology, but are transferable mathematical tools that combine and recombine across different practical applications; understanding these principles deeply, rather than memorising each experiment's specific procedure in isolation, is what allows a practitioner to understand, adapt, and even design new scanning approaches (like SfM itself, or the hybrid SfM+structured-light approach) rather than being limited only to the exact techniques explicitly taught
answers.c: SfM proves that all the earlier experiments in the lab were unnecessary prerequisites and could have been skipped entirely
answers.d: The purpose of including SfM as a final experiment is purely to increase the total number of experiments in the lab with no deeper pedagogical reasoning

explanations.a: Not quite. This directly contradicts the theory's explicit final section (Section 9), which specifically traces detailed, substantive connections between SfM and five separate earlier experiments (1, 2, 3, 4, and 8), demonstrating precisely the opposite of isolated, unrelated content — SfM is explicitly presented as a synthesis point drawing together concepts from across the entire lab.
explanations.b: Correct! This captures the deeper pedagogical purpose of positioning SfM as the lab's final, capstone experiment. Throughout the lab, concepts like triangulation (first introduced via simple two-camera stereo geometry in Experiment 1), reprojection error minimisation (first introduced in single-camera calibration in Experiment 2), point cloud representation (Experiment 3), correspondence-based geometric alignment (Experiment 4's ICP), and robust outlier-resistant estimation (Experiment 8's filtering) are each introduced within the context of one specific, relatively simple sensing scenario. SfM demonstrates that these are not narrow, technology-specific tricks limited to their original context, but genuinely general mathematical and geometric principles that can be extended, combined, and applied together in a substantially more complex scenario (many uncalibrated cameras, unknown poses, large-scale joint optimisation) to solve a considerably harder reconstruction problem. Recognising and internalising this transferability is what distinguishes deep understanding of 3D scanning principles from simply memorising a checklist of separate techniques — a practitioner who understands the underlying principles can reason about new sensing scenarios, hybrid approaches (like the SfM+structured-light combination), or entirely novel techniques not explicitly covered in this lab, by drawing on the same foundational toolkit developed across all ten experiments.
explanations.c: Not quite. This is contradicted by SfM's demonstrated dependence on concepts explicitly built up across the earlier experiments — rather than making earlier experiments unnecessary, SfM's successful use of triangulation, reprojection error concepts, correspondence matching, and outlier rejection demonstrates precisely why the earlier, more focused introduction of each of these individual concepts in isolation was pedagogically valuable, providing the necessary conceptual foundation for understanding SfM's more complex synthesis of them.
explanations.d: Not quite. This dismisses substantial, explicit pedagogical structure and connective reasoning that the theory document itself lays out in detail across multiple sections, particularly the closing synthesis in Section 9 — the specific, detailed connections drawn to five distinct earlier experiments represent genuine curriculum design intent, not arbitrary padding to increase experiment count.
